questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Practical CKAD tasks using ConfigMaps, env injection, probes, resources, and Service exposure. Demonstrates understanding of update strategies.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap usage via env/ENV
- Probes: readiness and liveness
- Resource requests/limits
- Service exposure and port mapping
- Rolling updates and rollout verification

## Code Example

```javascript
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config
data:
  PORT: 3000
  APP_MODE: prod

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
template:
  metadata:
    labels:
      app: api
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: api
      image: my-api:1.0
      ports:
      - containerPort: 3000
      env:
      - name: PORT
        valueFrom:
          configMapKeyRef:
            name: api-config
            key: PORT
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 3000
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 3000
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 200m
          memory: 256Mi

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you reload config without pod restart?
- How do you verify a rolling update complete with zero downtime?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a practical, namespace-scoped canary upgrade using standard CKAD tools: CronJob scheduling, patching Deployments, ConfigMaps/Secrets for config and credentials, and PVC-based logging. It also exercises InitContainers, probes, and network policy considerations in a real workflow.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and JobTemplate execution
- Patching Deployment images with kubectl set image or patch
- Reading image tag from ConfigMap and registry authentication via Secret
- Persisting status in a ConfigMap and logging to a PVC
- InitContainer to install tooling (kubectl, jq)
- Readiness/Liveness probes for the Job Pod
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting registry egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-upgrade
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: canary-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq; true"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          containers:
          - name: upgrader
            image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "set -e; CANARY_TAG=$(kubectl get configmap canary-config -o jsonpath='{.data.tag}'); kubectl patch deployment my-app -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"my-app","image":"myrepo/my-app:${CANARY_TAG}"}]}}}}' --record; echo done; sleep 1"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          imagePullSecrets:
          - name: registry-credentials
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to implement idempotent patches and roll back on failure?
- How to measure canary success (latency, error rate) before full rollout?
- How would this scale across many namespaces or deployments?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of admission webhooks, namespace-scoped control, and per-namespace policy management. It also touches TLS, RBAC, and logging considerations in Kubernetes.

## Key Concepts
- ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with NamespaceSelector

## Code Example
```yaml
# webhook Deployment skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-security-webhook
  namespace: webhooks
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ns-security-webhook
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-security-webhook
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: ns-security-sa

      - name: webhook

          secretName: ns-security-tls
```

```yaml
# ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with NamespaceSelector
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: ns-security-webhook-config
webhooks:
- name: ns-security.webhook.example.com
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: ns-security-webhook
      namespace: webhooks
      path: "/validate"

    resources: ["pods"]
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical drift detection in multiple namespaces, using PVCs, InitContainers and in-cluster API calls.

## Key Concepts

- In cluster tooling with InitContainers, Secrets, and PVCs
- Drift vs validation and how to compare live state
- Namespace scoped RBAC and NetworkPolicy
- Tooling: kubeval, kubectl, client-go in a container

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: drift-detector
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: drift-manifests
      - name: drift
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: drift-reports
      initContainers:
      - name: setup-tools
        image: alpine:3.17
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl kubectl kubeval"]
      containers:
      - name: detector
        image: drift-detector:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /manifests
        - name: drift
          mountPath: /drift
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 8080
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you implement rate limiting to avoid excessive API calls?
- How would you secure credentials and rotate secrets?

```yaml
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ns-backup
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  schedule: 0 2 * * *
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: restic-installer
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache restic']
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses familiarity with ConfigMap mounts, InitContainers, and sidecar reload patterns within a single namespace. It also evaluates understanding of signal-based versus in-process reload mechanisms, along with basic security practices using Secrets and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMap-driven runtime config**: Externalizing configuration allows updates without rebuilding containers
- **InitContainer provisioning**: Installing tooling (inotify-tools) needed by sidecars or main containers
- **Sidecar watching**: File change detection using inotifywait triggers graceful reloads without container restart
- **Signal-based reloads**: SIGHUP triggers graceful reloads; alternative approaches include local /reload API endpoints
- **Security with Secrets**: Sensitive data like admin credentials should mount via Secrets, not environment variables
- **NetworkPolicy**: Namespace-level egress restrictions limit exposure of internal endpoints

## Trade-offs
- **Signal vs. API reload**: SIGHUP requires the application to handle signals gracefully; /reload APIs add complexity but offer finer control
- **inotifywait vs. polling**: inotifywait is event-driven and efficient but limited to the container filesystem; polling works cross-platform but incurs overhead
- **Sidecar vs. embedded reload**: Sidecars keep concerns separated but add resource overhead; embedding reload logic reduces complexity but couples concerns
- **ConfigMap vs. volume plugins**: Native ConfigMap mounts require pod recreation for updates; external volume plugins enable dynamic updates at the cost of complexity

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD workflow patterns: CronJobs, batch processing, and secret management within a namespace; validates knowledge of init containers, sidecars, and network hardening.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling in a namespace
- InitContainer dependency installation
- ConfigMap for BATCH_SIZE
- Secret for API credentials
- Sidecar for TLS cert rotation
- NetworkPolicy for internal egress controls
- Probes for readiness and liveness
- Idempotency vs at-least-once semantics

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: csv-ingest
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-csvkit
            image: python:3.9-alpine
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'pip install csvkit && cp -r /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/* /shared/']
            volumeMounts:
            - name: shared-libs
              mountPath: /shared
          containers:
          - name: csv-processor
            image: python:3.9-alpine
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'python /app/process.py']
            env:
            - name: BATCH_SIZE
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: BATCH_SIZE
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: api-credentials
                  key: token
            volumeMounts:
            - name: data-pvc
              mountPath: /data
            - name: shared-libs
              mountPath: /usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /health
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /health
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 30
          - name: cert-rotator
            image: cert-manager/cert-manager-rotator
            volumeMounts:
            - name: certs
              mountPath: /etc/ssl/certs
          volumes:
          - name: data-pvc
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: data-pvc
          - name: shared-libs
            emptyDir: {}
          - name: certs
            emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  BATCH_SIZE: "10"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-credentials
type: Opaque
data:
  token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: csv-ingest-netpol
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: csv-ingest
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: data-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **CronJob vs Deployment**: CronJobs provide scheduled execution but lack continuous availability; Deployments offer always-on processing but require custom scheduling logic.
- **InitContainer overhead**: Installing dependencies at runtime increases startup time vs pre-built images, but provides flexibility for version updates.
- **Sidecar complexity**: TLS cert rotation adds operational overhead but ensures security compliance; alternative is using cert-manager injection.
- **Batch processing**: Larger batches improve throughput but increase memory usage and failure impact; smaller batches provide better isolation but higher API call frequency.
- **NetworkPolicy scope**: Namespace-scoped policies provide good isolation but require per-namespace management; cluster-wide policies simplify administration but reduce granular control.
- **Storage patterns**: PVC-backed storage ensures data persistence across pod restarts but requires careful volume management; temporary storage simplifies cleanup but risks data loss during failures.

```yaml
  name: audit-baseline
  namespace: example
data:
  baseline.json: |
    {"pods": [], "services": []}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-auth
  namespace: example
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: " collector-auth-token"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
  namespace: example
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-agent
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-agent
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: your-audit-image:latest
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do audit.sh; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: COLLECTOR_URL
          value: "http://collector.audit-system.svc.cluster.local:8080"
        - name: AUTH_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-auth
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
        - name: baseline
          mountPath: /baseline
          readOnly: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
      - name: tools
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: baseline
        configMap:
          name: audit-baseline
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: audit-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: collector
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Namespace isolation ensures audit agents don't interfere; NetworkPolicy provides security; PVC enables log persistence for compliance
- **Cons**: Each namespace requires separate Deployment (use Operator/Controller to automate); InitContainer adds startup latency; per-namespace RBAC management overhead increases with cluster size

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: multi-container pod design, InitContainers, PVCs, ConfigMaps, Secrets, TLS sidecars, probes, PDBs, and network policies, plus load validation and rollback strategies.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for tooling setup
- PVC mounting and data direction between /data/events and /data/enriched
- ConfigMap/Secret for runtime config and credentials
- TLS sidecar for certificate rotation
- Readiness and Liveness probes
- PodDisruptionBudget
- NetworkPolicy for scoped egress
- Load testing and rollback workflow

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: config-aggregator-config
data:
  batchSize: "100"
  enrichmentEndpoint: "http://enrich-controller.analytics.svc.cluster.local:8080/enrich"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: config-aggregator-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  apiToken: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-aggregator
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: config-aggregator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-aggregator
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq; sleep 0"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: myrepo/config-aggregator:latest
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: config-aggregator-config
            - secretRef:
                name: config-aggregator-creds
          volumeMounts:
            - name: events
              mountPath: /data/events
            - name: enriched
              mountPath: /data/enriched
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 9000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: 9000
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 10
      volumes:
        - name: events
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-aggregator-events-pvc
        - name: enriched
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-aggregator-enriched-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions

- What scaling considerations arise with batchSize tuning and backpressure?
- How would you observe and debug under intermittent enrichment endpoint failures?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD abilities: scheduling with CronJob, cross-resource coordination (ConfigMap/Secret), PVC usage, InitContainer setup, and NetworkPolicy scoping. It emphasizes per-namespace isolation and minimal instrumentation for reliability.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob per-namespace scheduling
- ConfigMap/Secret usage for config and credentials
- InitContainer provisioning of benchmarking tools
- Logs to PVC and metrics to ConfigMap
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for restricted egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: bench-endpoint
  namespace: {NAMESPACE}
spec:
  schedule: "*/15 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache wrk && sleep 1"]
          containers:
            - name: bench
              image: appropriate/curl
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "wrk -t2 -c50 -d30s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $BENCH_TOKEN\" $BENCH_ENDPOINT || true"]
              envFrom:
                - configMapRef:
                    name: bench-config
              env:
                - name: BENCH_ENDPOINT
                  valueFrom:
                    configMapKeyRef:
                      name: bench-config
                      key: endpoint
                - name: BENCH_TOKEN
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: bench-secret
                      key: token
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: bench-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle token rotation without restarting all CronJobs?
- How would you scale probes and tolerations to handle namespace density?
